opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd call it pretty scrappy and curiosity-driven. As an undergrad I didn't have a grand research agenda. I'd notice something interesting, usually about language, and chase it until it turned into a project.

A lot of it came from linguistics first and computation second. I've always cared about South Asian languages, things like Hindi, Urdu and Punjabi. Those languages are spoken by hundreds of millions of people but are badly under-resourced in NLP. So much of my early work was very hands-on. I built datasets, annotated data, and tried to document linguistic phenomena carefully. Then I asked how computational tools could help us understand them, or whether models were handling them properly.

The other big piece was working with people. I emailed researchers I admired and joined collaborations. I learned by doing, alongside people who were more experienced than me. I didn't wait until I felt "qualified" to start. I think that's the main thing I'd tell other undergrads: you learn research by doing research, even when your first projects are small or messy.

Looking back, the throughline was wanting to understand *why* things work, not just get a number on a benchmark. That instinct carried into what I work on now, which is trying to understand what's happening inside language models.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd characterize it as pretty scrappy and bottom-up. As an undergrad I didn't come in with some grand theoretical agenda. I came in as someone who loved languages, especially South Asian languages, and I just started building things. Datasets, lexicons, little annotation projects for languages that had almost no computational resources.

A lot of it was driven by a frustration that the field's attention was so concentrated on English and a handful of high-resource languages. So my instinct was: if the data doesn't exist for Hindi or Kashmiri or whatever, go make it. Get the linguistic details right, be careful about how you encode them, and then see what models can actually do with it.

The other piece was that I always tried to keep one foot in actual linguistics. Not just "does the benchmark number go up," but what does this tell us about morphology, about typology, about how these languages are structured. I think that combination of being very hands-on with data and very serious about the linguistic theory behind it is what defined that period for me. It was less about chasing the hottest architecture and more about asking good questions and doing the unglamorous work to answer them.

The starting point was a linguistic question: what pattern are we seeing, and what might explain it? Then I’d think about how to turn that into something we could test with data or a model. The interesting part wasn’t just whether a model performed well, but what its successes and failures could tell us about language.
